component.name: LecCheck
component.summary: Track the lectures, practices and labs you attend
מעקב אחרי הרצאות, תרגולים ומעבדות שהשתתפת בהם

description.p: Mark every class you attend during the semester and see your progress at a glance. LecCheck works offline and syncs live between your phone and computer.

ul.li: Today, Week and course pages with every lecture, practice and lab
Attendance requirements and statistics for each course
Reminders before class, and a quick question after it
Jewish and Israeli holidays as days without classes
English and Hebrew

ul.li: LecCheck for Windows is released. The Windows build is out and ready on GitHub: download LecCheck-2.0.0-beta.22-windows-setup.exe from this release's files (github.com/Emanuel4100/LecCheck2/releases). The setup, for 64-bit Windows 10 and 11, installs LecCheck for you without admin rights, and LecCheck then updates itself from inside the app. It's experimental and not signed yet, so Windows may say it protected your PC: choose More info, then Run anyway. Sign-in, sync, backups and Panopto work as on Linux; the window opens where you left it, and the title bar follows LecCheck's light or dark theme. No reminders on Windows yet. Uninstalling keeps your data.
More colors, and your own. Settings → Appearance has Teal, Amber and Indigo, and Custom: slide to any color and LecCheck builds its theme from it. Each device keeps its own choice.

Find a class's recording in Panopto right away. A search button by the recording link looks for that class now. When several groups were recorded, it asks which one is yours and remembers it; it asks before replacing a link you pasted; and when nothing fits it says why and lets you pick from that day's recordings. On the course page, Change switches a class to another group's recordings.

Panopto on all your devices, set up once. Signed in to LecCheck, your Panopto setup and sign-in are kept encrypted for your devices: the LecCheck server stores them but can't read them. On another device, Settings → Panopto recordings shows Set up on … with Use it here: check that both devices show the same 6-digit code and tap Allow on the first one. No Client ID, secret or browser on the new device, and every device looks for recordings (at most every 3 hours for all of them together). A device connected in beta.20 moves its connection in by itself. Disconnect works on this device or on all of them.

Importing a timetable from a chatbot asks for what's missing. The prompt has the chatbot ask first about the semester's dates, which group is yours when several are shown, course numbers and unreadable times. If its file still leaves something out, LecCheck asks you for it in the summary (dates, days, times, and optionally course numbers, which find Panopto recordings) instead of refusing the file.
A clearer Panopto setup guide, in English and Hebrew.

"Couldn't reach Panopto" no longer sticks. Android's daily look now waits for a connection, a look that failed without one tries again when you open the app instead of 3 hours later, and each read retries once after a dropped connection. Two rare ways to lose the Panopto sign-in during a refresh are fixed.

Panopto recordings, found by themselves (experimental). Settings → Panopto recordings connects LecCheck to your university's Panopto with an API client you create there once. It finds each course's folder by the course number and fills in each finished class's recording link, so missed classes show under Catch up on recordings by themselves. When several groups are recorded at the same time, the course page asks once which group is yours, with a suggestion. Found links are marked "Found in Panopto", and your own links always win. One connected device is enough: the links reach your other devices through sync. Android also looks once a day in the background. A meeting learns its group by itself when the links you pasted into it all point to one group. Removing a link asks whether Panopto may fill it (or, for a link Panopto found, whether it was wrong). In Developer mode, Matching details shows why each session got a link or not, and why each recording wasn't used. The tour offers to set it up.
Removing a recording link now keeps it removed (stored as an empty link) unless you let Panopto fill it, so a link found in Panopto doesn't take its place.

A change for one week only keeps following the meeting. Changing only the room for a week used to fix that week's time too, so moving the class later for every week left that week behind. Now only what you changed is kept.
Today is up to date as soon as you open it, instead of showing the time (or yesterday) from before the phone went to sleep for up to a minute.
"How was class?" for a late class is no longer skipped when it's due just after midnight.
Changing the semester's dates warns about every marked session it hides, including every-other-week classes whose weeks move when the start date does.

Sync is sturdier: after the server's data was reset, this device's data is offered again even if the app closed halfway; long Hebrew notes no longer make a sync too big for the server; a sign-in that was revoked is noticed right away; and a first sync applies its rows faster.
Reminders and backups: reminders are re-planned one at a time, so an older plan can't replace a newer one, and the daily automatic backup is written in the background without slowing the app.
Reception hours stay visible next to a class. A class at the same time used to cover the reception box on Week; now the reception hour becomes a thin strip beside it, named in its tooltip.
See which sessions have a recording or a note. Small icons show on session cards and, where there's room, on Week. The Today card has a Recording link button when one is saved.
All sessions filters and sorts. Show only sessions with a recording or a note, and sort newest or oldest first, by course, or with recordings first. Search finds recording links too.

A new status: Read the summary. Mark a session you caught up on by reading its summary. It counts like a watched recording: present in your stats, and toward a requirement when recordings count. On phones the status buttons now take two rows. Keys 1 to 6 mark a session on desktop. Older versions of the app show these sessions as unmarked until they update.

Days off are easier to spot. The day's name at the top of Week is tinted with the day-off icon, and the month calendar on desktop gives a day off its own tinted circle instead of fading it like a day outside the semester.
Cancel all classes on one day without making it a day off: tap the day's name on Week. The day gets the canceled stripes, and Undo or Restore classes brings them back.
A calmer way to mark a session. One Attended button with a menu for the other statuses replaces the green and red buttons; the color only shows once it's marked.
Today is less crowded: the session in the big card isn't listed again in the schedule.
Stats starts with your courses: overall attendance, then each course with its requirements under it. On phones the charts fold under More details.
Settings on phones is a short list of categories, each on its own page.
Days off stand out on Week: the whole day is tinted with its name at the top, and a new icon replaces the umbrella. The date stays visible.
A saved recording is one tap away: "Recording link" opens it, and Edit changes it.
Reception hours: turn them on in Settings → Courses, add them to a course like a meeting, and they show on Week as an outline. They never count toward attendance.

Import a timetable with a chatbot: copy LecCheck's prompt, give it to your own chatbot with a screenshot or file of your schedule, and bring back what it writes. It's checked and previewed, and only adds a new semester.
Clearer Hebrew: statuses read as nouns, like נוכחות and היעדרות, and other awkward wording is fixed.

Typing on desktop no longer loses letters. A key that's also a shortcut (T, the digits in a session's notes, Home, the arrows) was taken by the shortcut even in a text field, so the letter never appeared.
LecCheck looks for updates every time it starts, not once a day.
The countdown on Today shows days from 24 hours on, like "2d 3h".
Delete cloud data asks you to type DELETE first.
A Today button on Week, in words, takes you back to this week. The icon was easy to miss.
Ctrl+Z on Week undoes your last change: a move, a quick add or a mark.
The mouse wheel changes the week: Shift+wheel, a sideways scroll, or the wheel over the day names. The plain wheel still scrolls the hours and Ctrl+wheel still zooms.
Choose the tab LecCheck opens on, for each device, in Settings.
A keyring that doesn't answer can't stop a sign-out halfway.
Linux releases are only the Flatpak now: the tarball and install.sh are gone. Installs from 2.0.0-beta.15 move from inside the app.

LecCheck for Linux is a Flatpak, from its own repository (signed with its own key): flatpak install --user emanuel4100.github.io/LecCheck2/leccheck.flatpakref, or open that file in GNOME Software or Discover. It runs on the freedesktop runtime (about 300 MB, shared with other Flatpak apps) and updates itself from then on. This is the last version for install.sh.

Move to the Flatpak: LecCheck installed with install.sh offers the move on Today, in Settings and in a window when it starts. Signed in, everything syncs first and you sign in again in the Flatpak; otherwise save a backup and choose Import backup on the Flatpak's welcome screen. Then it installs the Flatpak, removes the old version (its data stays as one more backup) and opens the new one.

Updates through Flatpak: the update window shows Flatpak's progress, then Verified by Flatpak (the repository is signed), and Restart starts the new version. The first time, your desktop asks whether LecCheck may update itself. If you chose Deny, or a new version needs new permissions, the window says what to run instead.

A clearer update window: how big the download is before you start; a Check the file step you can watch, which reads the download back and checks it against the signed release, then checks itself off; What's new in its own box with a scrollbar, headings and bold, in English left to right in Hebrew too; and when something fails, what went wrong (no connection, not enough space, a file that doesn't match, Android's installer) instead of "Couldn't update".
Check now opens the update window when there's a new version.
Import backup on the welcome screen, for a new device or the Flatpak.

A sign-in kept by the keyring while the data folder was gone (a new install, or the Flatpak finding the old version's sign-in) looked signed in while nothing synced: an empty device now gets the account's data back, and one with data of its own stays signed out until you sign in.
The update window that opens at startup no longer closes again by itself when LecCheck moves on from its splash screen.
Linux no longer needs WebKitGTK or libsoup.
Settings → Developer → Copy diagnostics says how LecCheck was installed on Linux.
